Update on this we found the root cause of why the restart wasn't working.
The manual restart button/link had a real bug: it fired several server commands at once instead of one after another, so a restart could race against itself and leave Mongo stopped without ever actually restarting it  which matches what you saw (rebooting/Server Controls not bringing it back). That's fixed and going through testing now.
While testing on one of the affected environments, we also found that the "Generic Server" device record the restart button relies on to reach the server was set to inactive and pointed at leftover, unrelated configuration so even with the bug fixed, the restart had nowhere reachable to actually run against.
Could you check the following for both affected systems (Old Master and Askaris)?
In the app, go to Devices and look for an entry with type Generic Server and username root for each system.Check whether it's marked Active.If it's missing, inactive, or you're not sure — let us know which system(s) so we can get it created/activated with the right credentials.If neither system has an active Generic Server device, we've also added a fallback so the restart can run directly on the server itself without one — but having it properly configured is more reliable long-term (it's also used for other admin actions, not just Mongo), so worth getting sorted either way.

thanks for the logs that answers it. BCRemit's log is the exact same failure signature as Askaris ("MongoDB cannot start: Linux kernel versions 6.19 and newer has a known incompatibility..."), so this is one root cause hitting both systems, not two separate problems. And the dmesg -Td output coming back empty on BCRemit (no OOM entries) rules out memory pressure too consistent with what we saw on Askaris.
Confirmed root cause (checked against MongoDB's own tracking ticket, SERVER-121912, since closed with a permanent fix upstream): MongoDB's TCMalloc allocator violates a kernel ABI (rseq) that changed in Linux kernel 6.19+. Since MongoDB 8.0.5, Mongo deliberately detects this at startup and refuses to run rather than crashing unpredictably later that graceful "cannot start" message is that safety check doing its job, not a random crash.
Both boxes are on an affected kernel:
Askaris: 7.0.0-1011-gcp, mongod v8.0.21BCRemit: 7.0.0-1010-aws, mongod v8.0.23MongoDB's own guidance is that kernel 7.0.14 or later resolves the incompatibility (both boxes are currently below that). So the actual fix here isn't in our code, the restart button, or Mongo config it's the underlying OS kernel version on both VMs. Once the host kernel is patched to 7.0.14+, mongod should start normally on its own.
Given that's infrastructure-level (GCP/AWS image kernel patching), could you confirm who owns kernel/OS patching for these VMs so we can get both boxes moved to 7.0.14+? Happy to help verify once that's done. In the meantime the restart-button fix we already shipped plus having an active Generic Server device configured will keep manual recovery working if it happens again before the kernel is patched.

here is important information if we deploy License server to any other environment that LS need access to below mention ports for LS.The license server requires inbound connectivity from the client environment over TCP ports 80 and 443 to support client-to-license-server communication.
The GCP firewall rule should be configured to allow traffic on these ports only from the authorized client public IP address or CIDR range. Where a single client IP is used, a /32 CIDR should be configured to restrict access specifically to that source and avoid unnecessary public exposure.
The firewall rule should target only the network tag associated with the license server VM, ensuring that the access is limited to the intended instance.
Example configuration:
gcloud compute firewall-rules create <FIREWALL_RULE_NAME> \
  --project=<PROJECT_ID> \
  --network=<NETWORK_NAME> \
  --direction=INGRESS \
  --action=ALLOW \
  --rules=tcp:80,tcp:443 \
  --target-tags=<LICENSE_SERVER_NETWORK_TAG> \
  --source-ranges=<AUTHORIZED_CLIENT_PUBLIC_IP>/32For an existing firewall rule, replace create with update as appropriate.
Requirement: TCP ports 80 and 443 must be reachable from the authorized client environment to the license server for the required license communication.

issues.description:
In our current implementation when you add a device type “Azure” we are configuring the Graph API and Microsoft Office 365 Management APIs. In this guide we have more than 30 steps to follow and if the user only needs Microsoft Office 365 Management functionality there is no way those functionalities will work.

Attached the PDF as well.

When checked the source code against this guide what claude recommended that Microsoft Graph calls (graph.microsoft.com) — do NOT require steps 9–20

Here is the investigation report from Claude

Short answer: No, steps 9–20 can't be skipped — but only some features need themThe "Azure" device in BlockAPT calls two different token audiences with the same app credentials, and only one of them is gated by steps 9–20.
1. Azure Resource Manager calls (management.azure.com) — require steps 9–20This is the bulk of the "Azure" device's Subscriptions menu, all real and wired up in app/Classes/Azure.php / app/Icontrol/MyWsdl.php / routes/azureaccess.php — not UI mockups:
Subscriptions, Resource Groups, Virtual Machines (list/start/stop/restart/delete), Virtual Networks, Network Security Groups, Bastion Hosts, Network Watchers, Public IP Addresses, Storage Accounts, Recovery Services Vault, Route Tables, Snapshots, Log Analytics workspace mgmt, Activity Log, Access Control (role assignments), Resource Health, Advisor Recommendations, Locks, Tags, Run Commands, Cost Management.Getting a bearer token for resource=https://management.azure.com/ only needs the client ID/secret (steps 1–8) — that part works fine without steps 9–20. But ARM authorizes every call against Azure RBAC role assignments on the caller, not just a valid token. Without the Owner role assignment at the subscription scope, every one of these calls — even GET /subscriptions — will succeed in getting a token but fail the actual request with 403 AuthorizationFailed. So for this whole category, steps 9–20 are mandatory, not optional.
2. Microsoft Graph calls (graph.microsoft.com) — do NOT require steps 9–20These reuse the same app credentials but request a Graph-scoped token instead (resource=https://graph.microsoft.com/, hardcoded in code, ignoring the device's configured ARM resource URL):
Risky Users / Risky Sign-ins (AzureRepository.php)MFA/SSPR registration report (AzureRepository.php)Users sign-in activityOutlook users/mail/attachments/audit logs (app/Classes/Outlook.php)Azure AD users/groups/calendars/events (app/Classes/AzureActiveDirectory.php)OneDrive files/drives (app/Classes/OneDrive.php)Microsoft Graph doesn't check Azure subscription RBAC at all — it authorizes purely on the app registration's Graph API permissions + admin consent (the PDF's steps 21–36, and the OneDrive-specific steps). Findings from initial CyberShadows evaluation — flagging before demo commitment

Added a restart action to the task module. Restart stops and starts the Edgenexus services and leaves the appliance powered on, so it is a far less disruptive option than a reboot, which power cycles the whole device.
Until now the task module only offered reboot, so anyone wanting to clear a stuck service had no choice but to take the appliance down completely.

It returns success as true even when it rejects a request, and it marks an accepted restart with the same error flag it uses for a refusal. The only field that distinguishes them is the status text, so detection now reads that instead, checked against every response the appliance has returned including an unreachable device.
Power actions now report the appliance's own message rather than text written by the platform, so an operator sees exactly what the device said.

Added a Global settings page under Advance, in the same place the Edgenexus portal has it.

We are getting reading to fully onboard our first major MSP (Brilliant Tel:  )MSP have specific requirements for clarify and traceabilityThe use of our pivot intelligence framework Who What When Where How Action  is critical  to facilitate this:When an action is taken by BAP, e.g. playbook, tasks, pushing a rule, update a whitelist firewall, etc. the audit/details of the BAP action MUST always follow this framework so that the administrator has all the relevant information quickly and effectively (example screen shot attached where this information is missing and ultimately this is wasting administrator time finding it, the information Who What When Where How Action should be in the description)Pivot Intelligence Model (PIM) data framework with examples:
Who — example: actor, user, host, or principalWhat — example: object, asset, file, domain, or resourceWhen — example: time, sequence, and timing irregularityWhere — example: network or system locationHow — example: method, protocol, exploit path, or techniqueAction — example: observed or enforced outcomeThis information MUST be added throughout  BAP for:

Please prioritise accordingly.

1. Executive summaryThe Pivot Intelligence Model (PIM) is a semantic and operational framework for explainable cyber reasoning. It converts heterogeneous telemetry into a stable six-pivot event grammar, evaluates the relationships among those pivots, scores contextual risk, and maps the result to severity, confidence, and action. PIM is designed to sit between raw telemetry and operational response, making autonomous cyber defence more explainable, auditable, and commercially deployable.
The model matters because it shifts the unit of reasoning from isolated alerts to contextual event objects and incident chains. In practical terms, it gives BlockAPT PivotrixAI a coherent engine for detection, correlation, prioritisation, investigation, and controlled autonomous response.

2. Why this framework mattersSOC teams are overwhelmed by fragmented alerts and disconnected control planes.Static severity labels rarely capture the real contextual risk of a multi-step attack.Many AI security systems are difficult to explain to analysts, governance teams, or sovereign buyers.Autonomous response is commercially valuable only if its reasoning is defensible.
3. Canonical event modelEvery event is represented as a six-pivot contextual object:
X(e) = [Who, What, When, Where, How, Action]

Interpretation:
Who — actor, user, host, or principalWhat — object, asset, file, domain, or resourceWhen — time, sequence, and timing irregularityWhere — network or system locationHow — method, protocol, exploit path, or techniqueAction — observed or enforced outcomeThe Action pivot is the structural differentiator. It means the model captures not only what happened, but what was done or enforced in response, and then reuses that information in future reasoning.

issues.summary: VirusTotal Error When Searching on IP
issues.description:
A free VirusTotal account throws a forbidden error when the user scans an IP.  Searching domain/URL is no problem and returns results.
The same account has no problem getting results in VirusTotal itself so not a VT permission issue.
Other VT account devices work fine in the same Platform or will show the exceeded allowance notice upon occasion when that is the case.
Device details:
blockaptpoc
20ceb61e740661c477c4a19f64d1c950a0a3d4081be0531e29ad10da3814790f
Root cause:
When a user searches an IP, the app also tries to fetch some extra related data ("Related URLs"), but VirusTotal does not allow that API call on free accounts (see VirusTotal's documentation: ), which is normal and expected. Instead of just skipping that missing piece, the app treated it as a full error and redirected to an error page.
Solution:
Updated the code so that when VirusTotal blocks that extra API call, the app simply skips it instead of redirecting to an error page. The rest of the IP search results still display normally.
